recipe.history:
Bok choy — also spelled pak choi and known in Cantonese as 白菜 (baak choi, meaning white vegetable) — is a variety of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) that has been cultivated in China for over six thousand years, making it one of the most ancient continuously farmed vegetables in human history. Unlike European cabbages, bok choy does not form a tight head; instead it grows as a loose rosette of thick, crisp white or pale green stalks topped with glossy dark green leaves, and each part of the plant has a distinct textural and flavor identity — the stalks are juicy, mildly sweet, and crunchy with high water content, while the leaves are tender, slightly bitter, and take on a silky, almost buttery quality when exposed to high heat. Baby bok choy — the immature harvested form, typically four to six inches long — concentrates all these qualities into a more delicate package and is particularly prized for its tenderness and its dramatic visual presentation, the tight bundles fanning open like a flower when halved and grilled. Bok choy plays a foundational role in Cantonese, Shanghainese, and broader Chinese cooking, appearing in stir-fries, braises, soups, and steamed preparations, and serves as the nutritional backbone of many daily meals across China, providing calcium, vitamins A and C, and folate in abundance.

Bok choy arrived in North America with the Cantonese immigrant communities who came to California during the Gold Rush era and who established the first Chinese restaurants and grocery markets in American cities. For decades it remained largely unknown outside Chinese-American communities and their neighborhoods, available only in specialized grocery stores. The explosion of interest in Asian cuisines during the 1990s and the growth of Asian supermarkets and restaurants throughout American cities dramatically expanded its availability, and by the early 2000s baby bok choy was appearing on the menus of non-Asian restaurants as a fashionable side vegetable. Grilled baby bok choy — halved lengthwise and placed cut-side down on a very hot grill or grill pan until charred and tender — became a restaurant staple, the char adding a smoky bitterness that countered the vegetable's natural sweetness in a way that steaming or stir-frying could not. The sesame glaze — oil, soy, a little honey, toasted sesame — was the natural accompaniment, and this combination translated directly and powerfully to a burger context.

The first time someone put grilled bok choy on a burger in front of me I was skeptical in exactly the way that people are skeptical of any unfamiliar combination before they taste it. I was at a restaurant in the San Gabriel Valley of Los Angeles where the chef had grown up eating both Chinese family meals and American fast food and had decided, with the confidence of someone who understood both traditions deeply, that they should exist on the same bun. The baby bok choy had been halved, pressed onto a screaming-hot cast iron grill plate until char marks appeared on the flat face, then brushed with a sesame-soy glaze that caramelized into a lacquered coat. It sat on top of an 80/20 chuck patty that was clearly, visibly, beautifully medium rare, and the combination of char and crunch and sweetness and savor against the rosy, juicy beef was one of those eating experiences that recalibrates your understanding of what a burger can contain. I have been making this burger ever since, adjusting the glaze each time — more ginger one iteration, a little fish sauce the next, finally settling on a version that is bold without being overwhelming.

Grilled baby bok choy on a burger makes the case for medium rare more visually than almost any other topping. The bok choy arrives hot, charred on its face, glazed and fragrant with sesame, and it needs a resting medium-rare patty underneath it — warm, juicy, slightly yielding — to anchor it on the bun and provide the fat that carries the sesame-soy glaze flavors across the palate. An overcooked patty is too firm and dry to absorb or interact with the glaze; the burger becomes a series of separate elements rather than a unified composition. At 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit the patty's rendered fat and natural juices create a kind of receiving layer for the bold toppings, pulling them into the beef rather than letting them sit on the surface. The medium-rare temperature window is where this burger actually works. Every other temperature is a degraded version of the idea.
ingredients: For the grilled baby bok choy:
8 heads baby bok choy, halved lengthwise
Fine sea salt and white pepper
1/2 tsp chili garlic sauce (sambal oelek or similar)
1 tsp cornstarch dissolved in 1 tbsp cold water
4 slices Havarti or mild white cheese
2 scallions, thinly sliced on the bias
1 tbsp toasted sesame seeds for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the steam-bun-style rolls: Combine flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a stand mixer bowl. Add warm water, neutral oil, and rice vinegar. Mix on low until combined, then knead on medium for 8 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky.
2. Cover and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 portions, shape into tight rounds. Place on a parchment-lined steamer basket or baking sheet. Let proof 30 minutes.

3. For a steamed bun: Steam over boiling water for 12 to 14 minutes until puffed and cooked through. For a baked version: Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C), brush with oil, and bake 14 to 16 minutes until pale golden. The steamed version is softer and more traditional; the baked version has more crust.

4. Make the sesame glaze: Combine soy sauce, sesame oil, honey, rice wine vinegar, ginger, garlic, sesame seeds, and chili garlic sauce in a small saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a simmer, stirring. Add cornstarch slurry and stir for 1 to 2 minutes until the glaze thickens slightly and becomes glossy. Remove from heat. Set aside.
5. Make the ginger-miso mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, white miso, grated ginger, rice wine vinegar, sesame oil, and honey until smooth. Refrigerate until needed.
6. Prepare the baby bok choy: Halve each head lengthwise through the core to keep the halves intact. Brush the cut faces generously with neutral oil and season with salt and white pepper.

7. Heat a grill pan or cast-iron skillet over very high heat until smoking. Place bok choy cut-side down in a single layer. Press gently with a spatula. Cook undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes until char marks are visible and the cut face is golden and slightly caramelized.

8. Flip the bok choy and cook the rounded side for 1 minute. The bok choy should be tender at the core but still have some structural firmness in the stalks. Remove from heat, brush immediately with sesame glaze while still hot, and set aside.

9. Prepare patties: Divide ground beef into 4 portions (about 170g). In a small bowl mix the soy sauce, sesame oil, and garlic powder, then gently fold into the beef just until combined — do not overmix. Shape into 3/4-inch-thick patties with a thumb dimple. Season both sides with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.
10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3 minutes first side undisturbed.
11. Flip, immediately add a slice of Havarti to each patty. Tent with a dome. Cook 90 seconds to 2 minutes more.
12. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a rack for 3 minutes.
13. While patties rest, split buns and toast cut-side down in the pan over medium heat for 60 to 90 seconds.
14. Reheat the sesame-glazed bok choy briefly in the pan if needed — it should be served warm.
15. Assemble: Spread ginger-miso mayo generously on both cut faces of the bun.
16. Place the rested cheese-topped patty on the bottom bun. Lay 2 glazed bok choy halves on top, cut-side up, so the char faces show.
17. Drizzle a small amount of extra sesame glaze over the bok choy. Add pickled ginger slices and scatter sliced scallions and sesame seeds over the top.
18. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
